summary: This RFC introduces domain-style names, how they serve ARPA Internet mail and host addresses, and the protocol and servers that implement them. It is an early concept document for the Domain Name System. It was replaced by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

eli5.summary: Instead of remembering a long number for every computer, you use a name like a family tree. This note explains the first idea of how that naming system works.

questions: how did the original domain name system work
what is a zone of authority
subtitle: The 1983 concept paper that proposed replacing one central host table with a distributed, tree-shaped database of domain names.

tldr.problem: ARPA Internet host names were kept in one global table maintained by the Network Information Center, and its size and update rate were near the limit of manageability. Mail addressing was also becoming irregular.
tldr.mechanism: A tree-structured domain name space is stored by name servers, each holding complete data for a zone it is an authority for, and queried by resolvers. Records carry a type, a class and a time-to-live, and referrals lead to other servers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 882 describes the concepts only, with the formats in the companion RFC 883. It was obsoleted by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 and updated by RFC 973.

facts.label: Max label and length octets in a name

today: RFC 882 has been obsoleted by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and it was updated by RFC 973. Its companion that carries the formats is RFC 883. Treat it as an early statement of the concepts rather than a current specification.

sections.title: The Need for Domain Names
sections.content:
RFC 882, written in November 1983, introduces domain style names, their use for ARPA Internet mail and host address support, and the protocols and servers that implement them. It covers the conceptual framework and omits many uses, fields and details, which are given in RFC 883.

At the time, hosts were registered with the Network Information Center (NIC) and listed in a global table, the file HOSTS.TXT. The size of the table and the frequency of its updates were near the limit of manageability, so the RFC calls for a distributed database instead of a centralized one. Mail was a bigger problem: mailbox names cannot be centralized, and the many methods for locating a mailbox forced users to know several address formats and ad hoc tricks.

The RFC draws several design requirements from this: a consistent name space where names do not contain addresses or routes, a distributed database with local caching, a facility useful for more than one application, and name server transactions independent of the communications system, so that simple queries can use datagrams while updates use virtual circuits.
sections.eli5: When there were only a few computers, one big list of their names worked. As the list grew, keeping everyone's copy up to date became too hard, so this paper suggests sharing the job.

sections.title: Name Space, Name Servers and Resolvers
sections.content:
The proposed solution has three components.

  • The domain name space, a tree-structured name space in which each node and leaf names a set of information. A query names a domain name and the type of information wanted.
  • Name servers, which hold information about the tree's structure and its data. A server usually has complete information about a part of the tree, called a zone, and is an authority for it. It also holds pointers to other servers.
  • Resolvers, programs that extract information from name servers for user requests, either answering directly or following referrals. A resolver is typically a system routine, so no protocol is needed between it and the user program.

The design assumes the data changes slowly, that access matters more than instant consistency, and that updates percolate out with timeouts set by the distributor. Each organization responsible for domains is expected to provide redundant name servers. The RFC requires the iterative style of query handling, where a server refers the client onward, and allows the recursive style as an option. All data originates in master files edited by local administrators.
sections.eli5: There are three helpers. The tree is the family tree of names, name servers are people who know one branch really well, and resolvers are the messengers who go and ask the right person.

sections.title: The Domain Name Space
sections.content:
Each node and leaf of the tree has a label. Labels are not guaranteed unique, except the root, which has a null label. The domain name of a node is the path from the root, read left to right from most specific to least specific, with labels separated by dots when printed. Internally a name is a sequence of labels, each a length octet followed by an octet string, ending with a zero length byte for the root.

The total number of octets for labels and label lengths is limited to 255, so a printed name can be up to 254 characters. A domain is a subdomain of another if the other's name is the right part of its name; for instance A.B.C.D is a subdomain of B.C.D, C.D and D.

A special label * matches any single label, so *.ARPA matches FOO.ARPA but not FOO.BAR.ARPA. The tree is intended to parallel administrative organization, so each node can delegate authority for new subdomains.

The preferred syntax in Appendix 1 says a label starts with a letter, ends with a letter or digit, has only letters, digits and hyphens inside, and is 63 characters or less. Case carries no significance.
sections.eli5: A name is read like a mailing address in reverse: the most specific part comes first and the biggest part last. Everyone who owns a branch of the tree decides what hangs below it.

sections.title: Resource Records
sections.content:
A domain name identifies a set of resource information made of separate resource records (RRs). Each record has an owner domain name, management information such as length and timeouts, a two-octet type, a two-octet class, and resource data that always starts with a two-octet length. That length lets servers and resolvers hold and pass on records they cannot interpret. The data itself is limited only by a maximum length of 65535 octets.

The class identifies the data format, for example IN for the ARPA Internet or CS for CSNET. Because class partitions the data, the same type can have different data formats in different classes.

The types used in the examples are A (host address), MF (mail forwarder), MD (mail destination), NS (authoritative name server), SOA (start of a zone of authority) and CNAME (canonical name of an alias). An SOA record marks the start of a zone and is never cached, since otherwise it would create false zones. An NS record marks a delegation, the first name outside a zone.

Queries carry a QNAME, a QTYPE and a QCLASS. QTYPE may also be MAILA (all mail agent records) or * (any type), and QCLASS may be *. Responses to QCLASS=* can never be authoritative, since a server cannot know all classes.
sections.eli5: Each name has a little card file. Every card says what kind of fact it is, which network it is for, and the fact itself, so a server can pass along cards even if it cannot read them.

sections.title: How Name Servers Answer
sections.content:
If a query is for a name the server has authority over, it returns the data or an indication that the name or resource does not exist. Otherwise it returns a pointer toward an authoritative server, and a server that is not an authority can never return a negative response. Authority runs from an SOA record down until an NS record delegates it away. A domain must register with its parent, identify a responsible person and provide redundant name servers.

Name servers also return additional information in a separate response section, for example the address of a mail agent whose name appears in an answer, to save a second query. Requestors must not depend on it being present.

The CNAME record handles aliases. When a server does not find the wanted record, it checks for a CNAME with a matching class, includes it in the response and continues the query at the name it gives. Wildcards are handled separately: a * in a stored record never overrides an exact match, and the query's labels replace the * in the reply.

Servers may optionally support inverse queries, mapping a resource such as an address back to names, and completion requests, but all servers must understand both and may return an error response. The RFC says inverse queries cannot be guaranteed complete or unique.
sections.eli5: A name server answers what it knows for sure. If it does not know, it says who to ask next, and it never says that a name does not exist unless that name is on its own pages.

sections.title: Resolver Behavior and Caching
sections.content:
A simple resolver must know how to reach a name server, must set query classes that suit its clients, must chain through multiple name servers to reach an authoritative one, must be able to try alternate servers, and must report different failures such as an unknown domain name, an unknown resource, or no reachable authoritative server. It should guard against referral loops, for example by discarding referrals that do not match more of the query name than the referring server. When it uses datagrams it must recover from lost and duplicate datagrams.

Resolvers that cache records must remember each record's time-to-live (TTL), expressed in seconds with 16 bits of significance, and discard the record when that time has passed. If a resolver shares a database with a name server, it must decrement the TTL of imported records periodically, but not for records the server is an authority for.
sections.eli5: A resolver is a messenger who writes down answers, but each note has an expiry time. When the time is up, the note gets thrown away and the messenger asks again.
